To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) individual differences in both local efficiency during a working memory task and age are significant predictors of working performance; 2) decreases in local efficiency during a n-back task are associated with better working performance; 3) increases in local efficiency are associated with better performance in younger individuals but with worse performance in older individuals; 4) increases in local and global efficiencies during rest are not significant predictors of individual differences in working performance; and 5) there are significant group differences in local efficiency

local and global efficiency in the brain functional network were significant predictors of individual differences in working memory performance in young and older adults, and that the direction of these relationships depended on age.

(1) local efficiency is associated with working memory performance in aging, and (2) age-related decreases in local efficiency are not associated with decreased working memory performance in older adults.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of brain networks in cognitive function and how they are affected by aging.
the functional organization of brain networks during the working memory process in both younger and older adults.

the functional connectivity brain network changes associated with age-related differences in the working memory process and how these changes may be associated with individual differences in working memory performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
local efficiency is a better predictor of individual working memory performance than is global efficiency.

local efficiency of information transfer during the working memory tasks is a more robust predictor of working memory performance than is global efficiency, and that age differences in working memory are more likely to reflect differences in local efficiency than global efficiency.
age-related differences in local and whole-brain network efficiency are not significant predictors of age-related differences working memory performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
age-related decreases in brain network efficiency may contribute to age-related decreases in working memory performance.
age-related changes in working memory may be related to changes in the efficiency of information transfer within brain networks.
the brain network efficiency metrics we used to predict working memory performance in aging were not as effective as the metrics that we used in predicting working memory performance in young adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain networks that are engaged during working memory are different for young and old individuals, and that these differences may underlie age-related changes in working memory.
individual variability in working performance can be predicted by individual differences in local and/or global efficiency in both young and older adults.
the efficiency of information transfer in the brain is a significant predictor of individual variability in working-memory performance.
